hazards.name: Space Radiation
hazards.nasaText: Invisible to the human eye, space radiation is not only stealthy but considered one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight.

hazards.name: Isolation and Confinement
hazards.nasaText: Behavioral responses occur among groups of people far from Earth who are isolated and confined in a small space over a long period of time.

hazards.name: Distance from Earth
hazards.nasaText: Instructions, new supplies, medical care, and more become increasingly challenging to receive from Earth as astronauts venture deeper into space.

hazards.name: Gravity Fields
hazards.nasaText: Astronauts' entire bodies – muscles, bones, inner ear, and organs – must adjust to the new gravities encountered on the space station or their spacecraft, as well as on the Moon, Mars, and Earth once they return home.

hazards.name: Hostile/Closed Environments
hazards.nasaText: Maintaining a safe ecosystem inside a spacecraft presents unique challenges, from ensuring optimal temperatures, pressures, and lighting, to reducing noise, monitoring microbial communities, and tracking immune responses.

risks.name: Risk of Altered Immune System Responses
risks.nasaText: The stresses of spaceflight can awaken inactive viruses inside the bodies of astronauts, leading to rashes and other symptoms.

risks.name: Risk of Altered Sensorimotor and Vestibular Function
risks.nasaText: Astronauts can experience motion sickness, issues with hand-eye or gait coordination, and dizziness during gravitational changes.

risks.name: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations
risks.nasaText: Weightlessness alters blood circulation and how the heart and blood vessels function, potentially increasing the risk of cardiovascular events.

risks.name: Risk of Decompression Sickness
risks.nasaText: Transitioning from a pressurized spacecraft to a lower-pressure spacesuit can cause health and mission complications when dissolved nitrogen starts to bubble within body tissues.

risks.name: Risk of Host-Microorganism Interactions
risks.nasaText: Skin and gut microbiomes can change in space, potentially increasing the risk of crew members getting sick.

risks.name: Risk of Hypoxia
risks.nasaText: Following steps to avoid the bends during spacewalks elevates the risk of mild hypoxia, when oxygen levels in body tissues become lower than normal.

risks.name: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
risks.nasaText: A healthy, balanced diet is an essential element of crew health and performance.

risks.name: Risk of Injury and Compromised Performance from Spacewalks
risks.nasaText: Crew members must manage risks in the spacewalk environment, including decompression sickness, and low oxygen and high carbon dioxide levels.

risks.name: Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
risks.nasaText: All astronauts perform exercise during their mission to counteract losses in bone density, muscle strength, and heart and blood vessel performance.

risks.name: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
risks.nasaText: The structure of the eyes and brain can change with spaceflight.

risks.name: Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes
risks.nasaText: Without gravity, bones break down and become more brittle, boosting the chances of painful breaks.

risks.name: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders
risks.nasaText: Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth, and other intense space stressors may all take a toll on the mental health of the crew.

risks.name: Risk of Inadequate Teamwork
risks.nasaText: Selecting a crew that works well together is essential for mission success and safety.

risks.name: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
risks.nasaText: Stressors include chronic sleep loss, constant work demands, and irregularities in their internal biological clocks.

risks.name: Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support
risks.nasaText: Future crews on deep space missions must be able to live and work in an environment where they may face unexpected problems with software, vehicles, or other systems.

risks.name: Risk of Injury from Dynamic Loads
risks.nasaText: During landing activities, crews risk getting injured.

risks.name: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers
risks.nasaText: Crews exposed to radiation from space may be more likely to develop cancer.

notes.hazardRiskMapping: NASA's risks page groups risks by physiology, behaviour and radiation. The link from each risk to the five hazards is Team Asteron's reading of NASA's text, not a NASA table.
notes.systemsOps: Asteron's store-and-forward link and escalation report address part of this risk for medical information only.
notes.methods: direct = measured every check-in; self-report = the astronaut answers a yes/no or 1-5 question; context = explained on the Hazards page only; out-of-scope = needs suit, vehicle or lab data we do not have; core = what Asteron is built around.
